title: Aluminum Company of America v. Essex Group, Inc.
lead: ALCOA and Essex designed a long-term aluminum-conversion price to track changing costs within a tolerable range. When electricity costs broke away from the chosen index, the court faced a bargain that gave Essex inexpensive metal while imposing mounting cash losses on ALCOA.

actors.name: Aluminum Company of America (ALCOA)
actors.role: Company converting Essex’s alumina at its Warrick, Indiana, works.

actors.name: Essex Group, Inc.
actors.role: Customer seeking secure aluminum supply for wire manufacturing.

actors.name: Alan Greenspan
actors.role: Economist who assisted ALCOA in designing the pricing formula.

actors.name: Judge Teitelbaum
actors.role: Federal district judge issuing findings and conclusions after trial.

proceedings: After trial, the district court granted equitable price modification on count one, rejected alleged oral amendment and contractual termination on counts two and three, and dismissed both Essex counterclaims. The opinion promised a later order; the casebook reports settlement during appeal.
limits: The court applied the parties’ Indiana choice of law through Pennsylvania conflicts rules and predicted Indiana law where unsettled. This is a district-court ruling, not an Indiana Supreme Court holding or appellate affirmance. Loss figures are projections, not damages awards; the ceiling remained part of the modified price.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The parties negotiate a long-term conversion service
sections.cue: Why did Essex want this particular arrangement?
paragraphs: Essex Group wanted a secure supply of aluminum for expansion into wire manufacturing and competition with integrated producers. Negotiations with Aluminum Company of America (ALCOA) began in spring 1967 and produced the Molten Metal Agreement on December 26.

Essex would supply alumina, ALCOA would convert it to molten aluminum at its Warrick, Indiana, works, and Essex would collect the output. The term ran through 1983, with Essex entitled to extend through 1988. The arrangement was a conversion service, not an outright sale of ALCOA-owned aluminum.

The initial charge was fifteen cents per pound: five cents linked to a construction-cost index, four fixed cents, three cents of nonlabor production costs linked to the Wholesale Price Index–Industrial Commodities, and three cents tied to ALCOA’s local hourly labor costs. The total could not exceed sixty-five percent of a specified published aluminum market price.

sections.title: An elaborate formula seeks bounded protection from cost changes
sections.cue: What did both sides understand the indices would accomplish?
paragraphs: ALCOA developed the formula with economist Alan Greenspan’s help and examined how the nonlabor index had tracked its costs. It sought a stable return near four cents per pound. Essex studied index stability before agreeing.

The court later found that the parties contemplated ordinary variation producing approximately one to seven cents of return per pound, not a guaranteed four-cent annual profit. The indices, ceiling, favored-customer term, force-majeure provision, and extensive bargaining reflected efforts to limit risk.

Beginning in 1973, oil-price increases associated with the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and unexpected pollution-control costs sharply raised electricity expense, the principal nonlabor smelting input. The chosen index failed to follow. Annual profits became increasing out-of-pocket losses in 1976–1978, partly reduced by a temporary surcharge. The opinion’s table showed a 1978 loss of 10.484 cents per pound and a greater loss without the surcharge. Essex meanwhile obtained converted metal at a fraction of market value and profited substantially from selling surplus metal.

sections.title: Negotiations fail to resolve the divergence, and ALCOA seeks judicial relief
sections.cue: How serious did the court find the loss?
paragraphs: At a July 21, 1975 meeting, company leaders discussed replacing the nonlabor index with actual costs. ALCOA later alleged that they agreed to that change; Essex disputed agreement. The pricing dispute ultimately reached a federal diversity trial before Judge Teitelbaum.
Pennsylvania conflicts rules required honoring the contractual Indiana choice of law. Where Indiana authority did not resolve an issue, the district court predicted how Indiana courts would rule.

The court projected losses exceeding $75 million over the remaining possible term absent relief or an unforeseeable economic change. After accounting for earlier profits, it also described losses above $60 million across the entire agreement. Those were different-period projections, not damage awards. Essex pointed to about $9 million in cumulative profit by trial and the absence of expert forecasts. The court relied on established recent cash losses continuing under present conditions rather than speculative foregone market profits.

sections.title: The court treats the index’s limited capacity as a shared mistaken assumption
sections.cue: Why was this more than a bad forecast or unilateral error?
paragraphs: On count one, Essex argued that ALCOA had merely forecast future economics incorrectly, that any mistake was ALCOA’s alone, and that the formula’s drafter had accepted the risk by omitting a floor. Teitelbaum instead characterized the mistake as a present actuarial error about an elaborate risk-limiting device’s capacity to track costs within tolerable bounds.

Essex’s chairman understood that protective function even though Essex naturally wanted the best deal for itself. Shared knowledge of the material assumption did not require identical commercial motives or concern for ALCOA’s welfare. The assumption was basic to the unusually long agreement, and its failure substantially distorted the exchange.

The court considered express allocation, trade usage and common understandings, reasoned allocation where neither controlled, and conscious ignorance. The indexed price, ALCOA’s expertise and drafting, and lack of a floor placed ordinary variation on ALCOA. They did not establish assumption of every deviation regardless of magnitude or probability. Even exceptionally prudent parties, the court found, would not have expected an additional floor to be necessary. Acceptance of a calculated range differed from an unlimited gamble.

The court’s then-current Restatement drafts differed in numbering from the later final text. Its characterization remained a contested present-mistake theory; discussion of removing the word existing from a draft definition also acknowledged a comment excluding erroneous predictions.

sections.title: Extreme expense and defeated purpose provide additional grounds
sections.cue: What limits did the court place on impracticability and frustration?
paragraphs: The court also found impracticability and frustration. Like mistake, those doctrines concerned basic assumptions and allocation of risk, but focused on severe hardship. Higher costs ordinarily belonged to contract risk; relief required expense far beyond ordinary variation and loss not fairly undertaken. ALCOA’s severe out-of-pocket losses, extraordinary index divergence, and absence of fault satisfied that standard. Earlier cases denying relief involved smaller or inadequately proved losses or different allocation of foreseeable risks.

Impracticability concerned the extreme cost of performance. Frustration concerned ALCOA’s principal purpose of earning money instead of suffering serious losses. The court acknowledged that typical frustration cases involved more specific purposes and that commercial leases commonly assigned business-failure risk to tenants. It nonetheless rejected an absolute bar where a profit objective was gravely defeated under a bargain limiting the risk.
This did not make every lost profit grounds for relief. The court expressly warned that merely losing an opportunity to sell at a higher market price ordinarily would not suffice.

sections.title: Equitable modification preserves supply and retains the original ceiling
paragraphs: Essex correctly observed that traditional reformation corrected a writing that failed to record an antecedent agreement. The court acknowledged that this case was different. It used equitable restitution and modification to preserve the exchange and avoid unjust enrichment. Rescission would give ALCOA a market-price windfall and deprive Essex of secure supply; unchanged enforcement would assign the extraordinary losses to ALCOA.

The adjusted price was the lesser of A and B. A remained the original contractual ceiling. B was the greater of B1, the original indexed price, and B2, a price calculated to yield ALCOA one cent per pound under the accounting methods of exhibit 431. Thus the index still governed when higher than B2, while the ceiling still controlled even if it caused a loss. Both parties agreed during trial that the ceiling was appropriate if relief was granted, and ALCOA did not challenge it under the same mistaken-assumption theory.

B2 would be calculated quarterly. Interim invoices used the latest computation, with the next calculation correcting the previous quarter through refunds or added bills. ALCOA had to provide quarterly B2 statements whether or not that figure controlled and preserve detailed supporting records until two years after termination. Protection of underlying trade-secret information coexisted with records sufficient to enforce the remedy.

sections.title: The alleged oral amendment and termination clause do not supply additional relief
sections.cue: Why did counts two and three fail?
paragraphs: For the alleged 1975 oral amendment, ALCOA’s witness recalled acceptance and Essex’s recalled only willingness to consider the proposal. The court found both credible but held that ALCOA failed to prove agreement by a preponderance. It therefore did not decide the statute-of-frauds issue and granted neither discharge nor requested damages on that theory.

Count three invoked a side letter permitting termination if a final court determination classified the transaction as a sale of goods. Teitelbaum found a real service arrangement: Essex supplied and owned the alumina, bore taxes and transportation risks, and dealt separately with its Australian supplier despite ALCOA’s majority ownership of that supplier. Supply and conversion were intentionally distinct.

Independently, estoppel by contract prevented ALCOA from contradicting the side letter’s settled service characterization to obtain cancellation. The contemplated threat had been a third party’s Robinson-Patman price-discrimination challenge. The pricing mistake did not unsettle the parties’ separate understanding of the transaction’s character.

sections.title: The contract excuses interrupted deliveries and permits the later quantity adjustment
sections.cue: Why did Essex lose both counterclaims?
paragraphs: Essex first challenged reduced deliveries in 1977–1978. Extreme cold, generator failures, and coal-supply and associated labor problems interrupted the designated Warrick source. Section 24 excused affected performance. ALCOA notified Essex, reduced deliveries in proportion to lost operating capacity, resumed them as conditions improved, and allocated the reduction equally between Essex and its own ingot business. Metal available at other plants did not override the agreed exclusive source; prior performance also supported proportional allocation.

The second counterclaim challenged a fifteen-percent reduction in 1979. The court construed the quantity tolerance as reciprocal: Essex could nominate within fifteen percent of the nominal amount, and ALCOA could deliver within fifteen percent of that nomination subject to the nominal limits. Negotiators had rejected Essex’s proposed exclusive discretion. ALCOA’s delayed use reflected attempts to negotiate the price dispute, not acknowledgment that the option was unavailable. Its adjustment could restore deliveries to nominal amounts. Both counterclaims were dismissed.

sections.title: The findings grant modification but do not supply an appellate affirmance
paragraphs: On April 7, 1980, Teitelbaum issued findings and conclusions granting equitable modification on count one, rejecting counts two and three, and dismissing Essex’s counterclaims. The opinion stated that an appropriate order would issue rather than reproducing a later judgment. No separate opinion was written.

The casebook reports that the dispute settled while on appeal. That subsequent-history account does not establish appellate approval of the district court’s prediction of Indiana law. The opinion’s comparative appendix likewise described foreign approaches historically, not their present law.
